metadata.title: We Ask the AI Now: People aren't leaving search. They're splitting their questions, and that quietly changes how everything gets found.
metadata.topic: SEARCH & AI — TWO TOOLS, ONE QUESTION AT A TIME
metadata.register: Warm, simple, friendly -- short sentences, no jargon; fair and curious, and clear about which numbers come from which survey, per the user's explicit tone request.
metadata.note: Sourced from the user-supplied article 'We Ask the AI Now' (pasted directly in the build request; three references: Bain & Company, 'Why consumers choose an AI chatbot over a search engine' (Mar 20 2026; survey conducted September 2025); Caswell, Tom's Guide (Sep 3 2025) reporting a survey by the publisher Future; Crestodina, Orbit Media Studios, 'The AI-search adoption survey' (Mar 18 2026) -- see FACTCHECK.md). User asked for a 'Deep Explainer' at exactly 4:00. The toolkit's actual deep-explainer skill targets 5-10 min and requires ~20-25% of body beats to be pantry/archival stills sourced through a two-gate pipeline. Both conflict with this request: a hard 4:00 target, and the user's own note that no footage exists for this article. Built instead on the ai-explainer chassis (Claude composer cold open -> presenter intro -> body -> sources note -> handoff -> outro), reusing the all-self-generated Manim/Remotion approach and af_bella/@HumanitariansAI branding used on this user's other reels. The host self-introduction ('Hi, I'm Agrima') lives in its own B00B presenter-intro beat. HEDGING (per the user's explicit request): every number is labeled with its source (Bain, Orbit Media or Future) on its card and in narration; the Future survey is said to be from 2025; Bain's survey is said to be from September 2025; Orbit Media is said to be a web design and SEO company that ran its own survey; the 76% AI Overviews figure is said to be based on a study Orbit cites; the closing sources card and spoken note say the surveys measure different things and their numbers should not be compared directly; the opening scene is labeled an illustration, not a real case; the 'what this means for anyone who wants to be found' section is presented as the author's own observation. NO real brand or company logos (the search and chat icons are generic; source and product names such as Google appear only as plain text); every visual is a generated Manim graphic. The user's explicit tone request (warm, simple, friendly; fair and curious) is a deliberate departure from this chassis's default Teardown register -- disclosed here.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW -- ask shown answered; no self-intro here (see B00B)
beats.narration_text: I asked Claude to help me plan a weekend trip. It got me thinking about how we look things up.

props.command:
claude "plan a weekend trip for my family
  on a small budget"

beats.role_note: presenter intro -- 'Hi, I'm Agrima' + lead-in; doubles as the EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY beat
beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Agrima. Today: how we now split our questions between search and AI.
beats.visual_intent: presenter card: name, then a short lead-in

beats.role_note: illustration: planning a weekend trip; a few years ago a search for 'best things to do in Lisbon' and ten tabs; today the same question to an AI chat plus 'I have two kids and a small budget' and one answer in seconds; labeled an illustration, not a real case, but it matches something real -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: You're planning a weekend trip. A few years ago, you'd type best things to do in Lisbon, and open ten tabs. Today, you might ask an AI chat the same thing, add, I have two kids and a small budget, and get one answer in seconds. This is an illustration, not a real case. But it matches something real.
beats.visual_intent: illustration: a person with a phone and a simple map; 'a few years ago' ten tabs vs 'today' one AI answer; labeled 'illustration -- not a real case'

beats.role_note: Bain & Company, 1,500 US consumers: 56% mostly or always use search engines as their default tool, 16% AI chatbots; Orbit Media, March 2026, 1,110 US adults: Google use has not declined; 'usually use search' for research 22% -> 29% (2025 -> 2026), 'usually use AI chat' 35% -> 28%; two tools, pick by question -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: Search didn't disappear. It split. In a Bain and Company survey of fifteen hundred US consumers, fifty-six percent said they mostly or always use search engines as their default tool. Sixteen percent said the same about AI chatbots. An Orbit Media survey of eleven hundred ten US adults, from March twenty twenty-six, found Google use hasn't declined. The share who usually use search for research grew from twenty-two to twenty-nine percent. Usually using AI chat fell from thirty-five to twenty-eight.
beats.visual_intent: split-screen: a generic search bar on one side and a chat bubble on the other; stat cards: Bain 56% vs 16%; Orbit 22% to 29% and 35% to 28%; each labeled with its source

beats.role_note: Bain: top uses of chatbots among users -- 53% make complicated topics easier to understand, 47% step-by-step instructions, 45% brainstorming, 45% quick factual questions; Future survey (2025): 55% US, 62% UK use AI instead of search for certain tasks (vacations, fitness plans, gift ideas, tech fixes, product comparisons, emails); local searches the exception: 24% of Orbit's respondents preferred AI chat -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: What do we hand to the AI? Bain asked chatbot users: making complicated topics easier to understand, fifty-three percent. Step-by-step instructions, forty-seven. Brainstorming and quick factual questions, forty-five each. A separate Future survey, from twenty twenty-five, found fifty-five percent of US respondents, and sixty-two percent in the UK, use AI instead of search for some tasks. The exception is local searches. Only twenty-four percent of Orbit's respondents preferred AI chat for those.
beats.visual_intent: a bar chart of the four Bain uses (53/47/45/45); a Future card (55% US, 62% UK, 2025) with task chips; an Orbit card 24% local searches; each labeled with its source

beats.act: BEAT 4 — the answer is at the top
beats.role_note: Orbit: Google's AI Overviews appear in 76% of search results pages (a study Orbit cites); in its survey 70% use AI summaries at least occasionally, ~23% ignore them, 7% have turned them off; Bain: 46% of respondents use AI overviews from search engines; search engines summarize, AI tools search, the line blurs -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: The answer is now at the top of the page. Orbit reports that Google's AI Overviews appear in seventy-six percent of search results pages, based on a study it cites. In its survey, seventy percent use AI summaries at least occasionally, about twenty-three percent ignore them, and seven percent have turned them off. Bain found forty-six percent of its respondents use AI overviews. Search engines now summarize, and AI tools now search.
beats.visual_intent: a generic results page with a summary box at the top and a list of links below; stat cards 76% (a study Orbit cites), 70% / 23% / 7% split bar (Orbit survey), 46% (Bain)

beats.role_note: Bain: 76% of baby boomers and 55% of Gen X mostly or always use search engines, vs 42% for both millennials and Gen Z; if habits follow age the mix will keep shifting -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: Younger people lead the way. In Bain's survey, seventy-six percent of baby boomers, and fifty-five percent of Gen X, mostly or always use search engines. For millennials and Gen Z, it's forty-two percent for both. If habits follow age, the mix will keep shifting.
beats.visual_intent: a simple bar chart comparing generations (boomers 76%, Gen X 55%, millennials 42%, Gen Z 42%), labeled Bain

beats.role_note: Orbit: 49% agreed they trust Google's results more than AI chat; 36% unlikely to ever trust AI chat tools; 44% said AI has changed how they look for information; adopting the tools while keeping a healthy amount of doubt -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: Trust is still catching up. In Orbit's survey, forty-nine percent agreed they trust Google's results more than AI chat, and thirty-six percent are unlikely to ever trust AI chat tools. Yet forty-four percent said AI has changed how they look for information. People adopt the tools, with a healthy amount of doubt.
beats.visual_intent: a 'trust meter' graphic: three gauges (49% trust Google's results more than AI chat, 36% unlikely to ever trust AI chat tools, 44% say AI changed how they look), each labeled Orbit Media

beats.role_note: the author's own observation: when the answer comes first and the websites second, being clear and easy to find matters more; hotel, gallery, shelter, small shop; Orbit's author lists what won't change: informative websites, original research and genuine points of view, word of mouth, live events and communities, email, influencer marketing; the tools change, the goal stays -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: What this means for anyone who wants to be found. This is my own observation: when the answer comes first, and the websites come second, being clear and easy to find matters more than ever. For a hotel, a gallery, a shelter, or a small shop. Orbit's author lists what won't change: informative websites, original research, word of mouth, live events and communities, email, and influencer marketing. The tools change. The goal of helping people who need you stays.
beats.visual_intent: generic icons (hotel, gallery, shelter, shop) labeled 'my observation'; a list of six things that won't change labeled 'Orbit's author'; closing line: the tools change, the goal stays

beats.role_note: closing idea: not one tool replacing another; we choose a tool depending on the question; directions to a coffee shop -> search; a complicated idea in plain words or a trip planned around the family -> ask the AI; typing keywords and scanning ten blue links is becoming one of several ways -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: The big shift isn't that one tool replaced another. It's that we choose a tool depending on the question. Directions to a coffee shop? Search. A complicated idea explained in plain words, or a trip planned around your family? Ask the AI. Typing keywords and scanning ten blue links is slowly becoming just one of several ways we look for answers.
beats.visual_intent: a person choosing between two generic tools depending on the question: 'directions to a coffee shop' -> search; 'a complicated idea in plain words' and 'a trip planned around your family' -> AI chat; closing line

beats.role_note: Orbit Media is a web design and SEO company and ran its own survey; the Future survey is from a media publisher; Bain's survey was conducted in September 2025; the surveys measure different things so their numbers should not be compared directly; the opening scene is an illustration -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: A note on sources. Orbit Media is a web design and SEO company, and ran its own survey. The Future survey is from a media publisher. Bain's survey was conducted in September twenty twenty-five. These surveys measure different things, so don't compare their numbers directly. And the opening scene is an illustration.
beats.visual_intent: a sources card (three references as plain text, no logos) with on-screen notes: Orbit Media = web design and SEO company, own survey; Future = media publisher (2025); Bain = September 2025; different measures, do not compare numbers directly; opening scene is an illustration

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW -- suggested prompt typed in, viewer-addressed, read aloud and discussed
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Next time you have a question, notice which tool you reach for, and why.

props.command:
claude "search or AI chat for this question?
  which fits better, and why?"
